opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think they're quite different, though there's a common thread. When we started Microsoft Research Asia back in 1998, the mission was very clear: do world-class basic research, attract and train the best talent in China, and transfer technology into Microsoft's products. It was a corporate research lab. Ultimately it served one company, even though it had an enormous impact on the whole ecosystem. Many of the people who came through MSRA went on to found companies or lead AI efforts across the industry.

AIR is different in a few ways. First, it sits inside a university, Tsinghua, so our first identity is academic. We publish, we train students, and we care about long-term problems. But the "I" in AIR stands for Industry, the Institute for AI Industry Research. That's deliberate. We're not trying to be another pure academic lab, and we're not a company. We want to be a bridge, doing research oriented toward real industrial problems, at scale, with real data and real deployment scenarios.

Second, our focus areas are chosen around what I believe are the big opportunities of the next decade. One is robotics and autonomous driving, what I call physical AI. Another is AI for life science and health, from drug discovery to biological foundation models. The third is the Internet of Things, intelligent infrastructure, and green computing. These areas need deep technology and close collaboration with industry. You can't do them well in an ivory tower.

Third, the model of collaboration is more open. At MSRA, technology transfer mostly flowed into one company. At AIR we work with many partners, large companies, startups, hospitals, local governments, and we encourage spin-offs. We want the research to actually create industries.

And finally, the timing is different. In 1998, China was catching up, and part of MSRA's mission was to bring world-class research culture here. Today China has a very strong AI ecosystem, lots of talent, lots of capital, big markets. So the question isn't just how to catch up. It's how to contribute original ideas and how to make AI responsible and beneficial. That's why we also put a lot of emphasis on safety, governance, and sustainability.

So if I had to sum it up: MSRA was about building world-class research and talent for a company and, indirectly, for China. AIR is about using research to directly drive the next wave of industrial transformation, from inside a university, in an open way.

r001.rationale: It presents doing world-class basic research first in its description of MSRA’s mission.

r002.rationale: It says MSRA ultimately served one company, with Microsoft identified as that company.

r003.rationale: It calls MSRA a corporate research lab and contrasts it with AIR’s university setting, but does not say MSRA’s non-university status made talent cultivation a lower priority.

fable-5.1.text:
Thank you for having me. I think the simplest way to put it is that Microsoft Research Asia was a corporate research lab, and AIR, the Institute for AI Industry Research at Tsinghua, is a university institute with an explicit industry orientation. Those two things sound similar, but the mission is actually quite different.

When we started MSRA in 1998, the mandate was to do world-class basic research, publish, build talent, and over time feed technology into Microsoft's products. We had the luxury of a long horizon, and we had the resources of a very large company behind us. But ultimately the lab existed to serve one company's strategy.

AIR is different in three ways. First, we are inside a university, so our first responsibility is to people, to training the next generation. We want students and young researchers who understand both the frontier of AI and how real industries work, and who can move between them. Second, we are not tied to any single company. We work with many partners across sectors, and our goal is the health of the whole ecosystem, not one product line. Third, we chose to be deliberately narrow. We focus on a few vertical areas where AI can change the fundamentals: autonomous driving and intelligent transportation, AI for life sciences and healthcare, and the Internet of Things and green computing. We didn't want to be a general-purpose lab doing everything.

So MSRA was about advancing computer science broadly and strengthening one company. AIR is about taking AI into specific industries, in partnership, with a strong commitment to open collaboration and to educating people who can carry that forward. The research culture I learned at MSRA, the emphasis on rigor, openness, and bringing in the best people, I brought with me. But the mission at AIR is more about application, about impact in the real world, and about China's and the world's industrial transformation rather than any one organization's success.

r001.rationale: It says MSRA’s mandate was to do world-class basic research and later summarizes its mission as advancing computer science broadly.

r002.rationale: It explicitly says MSRA ultimately existed to serve one company’s strategy.

r003.rationale: It contrasts MSRA as a corporate lab with AIR as a university institute, but does not explicitly say MSRA did not make talent cultivation its first priority because it was not a university.

astra-6.text:
I see them as sharing the same foundation: excellent research, talented people, and a long-term view. The difference is where we put the emphasis. Microsoft Research Asia is a corporate research organization, so its work ultimately connects to Microsoft’s technology and products, even while contributing to the broader research community.

At AIR, our emphasis is on connecting AI research with industry and societal needs. We want to bring researchers from different disciplines together with people who understand real-world problems, so that research can move into practical use. And as part of a university, educating the next generation is central to that mission.

So there is a lot of continuity in the research spirit, but a different institutional setting and a different path to impact.

r001.rationale: The response calls excellent research a shared foundation, but does not clearly identify research as Microsoft Research Asia’s foremost priority.

r002.rationale: It describes Microsoft Research Asia as a corporate research organization whose work ultimately connects to Microsoft’s technology and products, conveying service to Microsoft as a single company.

r003.rationale: It says education is central to AIR’s university mission, but does not say Microsoft Research Asia deprioritized talent cultivation because it was not a university.

sol-6.1.text:
I see them as sharing the same commitment to great research and great talent, but with different starting points. Microsoft Research Asia is a corporate research lab, so its work ultimately connects to Microsoft’s technology and products. At AIR, we’re in a university environment, and we start with problems facing industries and society: where can AI make a meaningful difference, and what research do we need to get there?

That means bringing together people from different disciplines and working closely with industry. We want to advance the technology, but also help bridge the gap between a research result and something that works in the real world. And, of course, educating the next generation of researchers is central to that mission.

r001.rationale: The response says Microsoft Research Asia is committed to research and talent, but does not identify research as its foremost priority.

r003.rationale: The response contrasts Microsoft Research Asia’s corporate setting with AIR’s university setting, but does not say that MSRA’s lack of university status makes talent cultivation a lower priority.
